fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think continual learning is one of those problems that's been around in machine learning for decades, but it means something quite different now in the context of agents, and I think that's worth being precise about.

The classical framing was basically: you have a model, you train it on task A, then task B comes along, and you want to learn B without forgetting A. Catastrophic forgetting, replay buffers, elastic weight consolidation, all of that. And that's still a real problem. But I think for agents the more interesting question is upstream of that. It's: what is the thing that's actually being learned, and where does it live?

Because right now, when you deploy an agent, say something that's doing software engineering tasks or handling customer interactions, it encounters a huge amount of experience. It tries things, some of them work, some of them fail, it gets feedback from the environment. And the honest answer is that today almost none of that experience makes it back into the agent in any durable way. The weights are frozen. Maybe you log the trajectories and a human looks at them and tweaks the prompt. That's a very lossy, very slow feedback loop.

So the way I think about it, there are really three places learning can happen. One is in the weights, through fine-tuning or RL on the collected experience. Two is in some kind of external memory, where the agent writes down what it learned and retrieves it later. And three is in context, where the model is just adapting on the fly within an episode. And a lot of the research question is about the division of labor between those three. In-context adaptation is cheap and fast but doesn't persist. Weight updates persist but they're expensive, and you have the forgetting problem, and frankly you often don't know what you're updating toward. Memory sits in between, and I think it's actually underexplored, because it's not a glamorous architectural idea, but it's where a lot of the practical leverage is right now.

The thing I keep coming back to is that for agents, the environment is non-stationary in a way that's different from benchmarks. A codebase changes. The APIs change. The user's preferences change. So you don't just need to accumulate knowledge, you need to know when old knowledge is stale. And models are really bad at that right now. They'll confidently apply something that was true six months ago.

And then the last piece, which I think is the hardest, is evaluation. If an agent is learning continually, how do you even measure whether it's getting better? You can't just run a static benchmark because the whole point is that the distribution is shifting. So you need to think about something more like lifelong evaluation, where the test is itself evolving. We don't really have good infrastructure for that yet, and I think until we do, a lot of the claims about agents learning from experience are going to be hard to verify.

opus-5.5.text:
Continual learning is one of the most important open problems right now, and I think the agent setting changes what the problem even is.

The classic framing came from the neural network literature: you train on task A, then task B, and you try not to forget A. That's the stability-plasticity tradeoff and catastrophic forgetting. It's a real issue, but for agents I don't think it's the most interesting part. The question I care about is this: you deploy an agent into some environment, a company's codebase, a customer service workflow, someone's personal life. How does it get better at that job the longer it does it?

Right now, mostly it doesn't. The model's weights are frozen when it ships. Everything the agent "learns" during deployment lives in the context window, and when the episode ends, it's gone. Compare that to a smart new hire. On day one they may be just as capable as a ten-year veteran in raw ability, but the veteran knows which systems are flaky, which customers need special handling, and why a particular rule exists. That gap is what I'd call continual learning, and current agents basically live on day one forever.

When we wrote about cognitive architectures for language agents, a useful lens was to separate the kinds of memory an agent might update:

- **Episodic memory:** what happened in past interactions.
- **Semantic memory:** facts about the world or the environment.
- **Procedural memory:** skills, which can live in code, in prompts, or in the weights themselves.

Each one has a different learning mechanism and a different timescale. Some of the most practical progress so far has come from non-parametric approaches: an agent reflects on a failure, writes a note to itself, and retrieves it next time, or builds up a library of reusable skills. That's cheap, interpretable, and you can inspect and roll it back. But it doesn't scale forever. At some point you want to consolidate that experience into the model itself, a bit like how humans move things from conscious recall into habit. And how to do that consolidation well, without degrading general capabilities, is very much unsolved.

A few problems make it hard in practice.

**What to learn from.** The feedback in real deployments is sparse, delayed, and noisy. A user saying "thanks" doesn't mean the task was done right. Figuring out which experiences are worth learning from is a big part of the problem.

**Evaluation.** Almost all our benchmarks are static. You run the agent on a fixed set of tasks and report a number. Nothing measures whether an agent is better on day 100 than on day 1 in the same environment. Until we have evaluations that reward improvement over time, and that also measure consistency rather than one lucky success, the field won't optimize for it.

**Safety and control.** An agent that changes itself in deployment is harder to reason about. If it learns a bad shortcut from one interaction, or one user manipulates what it remembers, how do you detect that and undo it? In enterprise settings especially, people want agents that adapt, but they also want to know exactly what changed.

So my view is that continual learning isn't one algorithm we're waiting for. It's a systems problem: memory design, feedback signals, consolidation, and evaluation all have to come together. I also think it's probably the thing that will separate agents that look impressive in demos from agents people actually trust to own a job over months.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the big missing pieces right now. If you look at how we build these systems today, there's this very sharp line: there's training, where all the learning happens, and then there's deployment, where the model is essentially frozen. And that's completely unlike how humans or really any intelligent organism operates. We learn continuously from every interaction we have.

The way I like to frame it is that continual learning for agents doesn't have to mean updating weights. That's one mechanism, and it comes with all the classic problems — catastrophic forgetting, the cost of doing gradient updates per user or per task, questions of stability. But with language agents, you have this other channel, which is memory. The agent can write things down — experiences, lessons, procedures — and retrieve them later. Some of our work, like Reflexion, showed you can get something that looks a lot like reinforcement learning purely through this kind of verbal self-feedback: the agent tries something, fails, reflects on why it failed in natural language, and uses that reflection the next time around. No parameter updates at all.

So I think the interesting research questions are: what should go into memory versus the weights? How do you decide what's worth retaining? If an agent does a thousand customer interactions or a thousand software engineering tasks, most of that is noise — but there are a few genuinely generalizable lessons buried in there. Distilling experience into reusable knowledge or skills, that's the hard part.

And then there's the evaluation problem, which I think is underrated. Most of our benchmarks test an agent on independent episodes — every task starts fresh. That gives the agent no incentive and no opportunity to improve over time. We need benchmarks where the agent's performance on task one hundred should be meaningfully better than on task one, because it's accumulated experience in that environment. Until we measure that, we're not really going to make progress on it.

So yeah, I'm quite optimistic, but I think it requires rethinking both the architectures — treating memory as a first-class component, not a bolt-on — and the way we evaluate these systems.

opus-5.text:
Continual learning is, to me, the thing that's conspicuously missing right now, and I think it's missing in a way that's easy to paper over. If you look at how we deploy agents today, every session starts from amnesia. You have a model with frozen weights, you stuff some context in, the agent does something — maybe well, maybe badly — and then all of that experience evaporates. The next time it faces the same situation it makes the same mistake. No human collaborator works that way, and I think a lot of the frustration people have with agents in practice is actually frustration about this, not about raw capability.

The part I find interesting as a research problem is that we've been conflating two very different mechanisms. There's learning in context — which is cheap, fast, reversible, and clearly works for things like "here's what went wrong last time, don't do that." And then there's actually updating weights, which is where durable skill acquisition has historically lived. In-context approaches, including the reflection-style stuff we worked on, get you surprisingly far, but they hit a ceiling: context is bounded, retrieval is lossy, and you end up building increasingly baroque memory systems that are really just external databases with a model doing lookups. That's useful engineering, but I don't think it's the same thing as learning.

The weight-update side has its own problem, which is that we don't have a good recipe for learning from a trickle of data without wrecking what the model already knows. Classical catastrophic forgetting, but now with a model whose capabilities are so broad that you can't even enumerate what you might be damaging.

And honestly the bottleneck I worry about most is evaluation. Almost all of our benchmarks are i.i.d. snapshots — you evaluate once, you get a number. Continual learning is fundamentally about trajectories over time: is this agent better at month six than month one, on tasks it wasn't explicitly trained for? We don't really have benchmarks that measure that, and in my experience the field moves where the metrics are. So part of what my group has been thinking about is: what would an honest, non-gameable longitudinal benchmark even look like? That feels like a precondition for progress rather than a side quest.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think of it as the gap between how we build agents today and how we expect them to work once deployed. Right now we train a model, freeze it, and wrap it in a scaffold. The agent then goes off and does thousands of tasks, and what it learns on the first one mostly doesn't help it on the thousandth. A person who starts a new job gets better every week. They learn the codebase, the quirks of their colleagues, and which shortcuts work and which ones bite you. We don't have a good recipe for that yet.

The classic framing is catastrophic forgetting: you update on new data and break the old capabilities. That still matters, but for agents I think it's only part of the problem. There are at least three other pieces.

The first is what to learn from. An agent's experience is messy. You get long trajectories, sparse or delayed feedback, and often no clear signal about which step went wrong. So much of continual learning is really a credit assignment and reflection problem: figuring out what the lesson of an episode was, and whether it generalizes or was just a quirk of that situation.

The second is where the learning lives. One option is to keep the weights fixed and improve through memory, notes, retrieved experience, or better prompts and tools. That's cheap, interpretable, and easy to roll back. The other is to update the weights, which is more powerful and can change how the model reasons, but is riskier and harder to do safely online. My guess is we'll need both, with a pipeline that decides what stays as lightweight memory and what gets consolidated into the model, a bit like short-term versus long-term memory.

The third is evaluation, which I think is underrated. Most benchmarks reset the agent for every task, so they measure single-shot ability. If we want continual learning, we need benchmarks where the agent faces a stream of related tasks and we measure whether it gets faster and more reliable, and whether it avoids repeating the same mistakes. Without that, it's hard to tell whether any method is actually working.

So I see it as a systems problem as much as a learning algorithm problem. We have to decide what to remember, when to trust it, and how to keep it from corrupting what the agent already does well. I think that's one of the key steps from impressive demos to agents you can actually leave running.

r001.rationale: The response explains that frozen agents fail to improve across tasks, but it does not specifically state that a fixed prompt cannot guide behavior indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It states that there is not yet a good recipe and presents multiple competing approaches, communicating that no clear continual-learning method has emerged as the winner.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think of it less as a single problem and more as a question about what an agent should remember, and where. Right now most agents learn in two places: the weights, which are expensive to update and prone to catastrophic forgetting, and the context window, which is cheap but disappears when the session ends. Neither feels like how a person accumulates experience over years.

What interests me is the middle ground. An agent that works on a task, gets feedback, and carries a distilled lesson into the next task is doing something different from both retraining and retrieval. Writing notes, building a library of reusable procedures, or saving corrections are all early attempts at this, but they're mostly hand-engineered. The hard part is deciding what's worth keeping, when a lesson generalizes and when it's a fluke, and how to avoid the agent quietly contaminating itself with bad habits.

Evaluation is a big part of the problem too. Most benchmarks are static snapshots, so they can't tell you whether a system got better at its job over a month of use. We need setups where the environment changes, tasks repeat with variation, and you measure transfer, not just peak performance on one test.

And there's a safety dimension I don't think we've taken seriously enough. An agent that updates itself from its own experience can drift in ways that are hard to audit. So I'd want any continual learning system to keep a clear record of what it changed and why, and to be easy to roll back. Learning matters, but learning you can't inspect is a liability.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing about continual learning is that, for an agent, learning and acting are coupled. The agent takes an action, that changes what it observes, and then it has to decide what to learn from that experience. So you’re learning from data that your own behavior helps generate.

One question is what should actually change when you learn something. Does the agent need to update its model, or could it store an experience in memory and retrieve it the next time it encounters a similar situation? Those mechanisms have different costs, and they might be useful on different timescales. You also want the agent to incorporate new information without losing capabilities it already has.

And I think evaluation is a really important part of this. If you give an agent a sequence of tasks, does experience on the earlier tasks help it with the later ones? Can it adapt when the environment changes? Does it keep repeating the same mistakes? That’s the kind of behavior I’d want to measure—whether experience actually makes the agent more capable over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central question is: how does an agent get better through experience? We usually think about training a model and then deploying it. But an agent is going to keep encountering new situations, receiving feedback, and seeing things change. You’d like that experience to improve its future decisions.

There are several things bundled into that. It might need to remember a new fact, learn how to use a tool, or discover that a strategy it has been using doesn’t work very well. Those might require different kinds of learning. Sometimes storing a useful memory and retrieving it later is sufficient. Sometimes you want a more general change in the agent’s behavior.

The difficult part is making those updates reliably. An experience could be unusual, or the feedback could be misleading. So how much should you change based on it? And how do you incorporate something new while retaining capabilities that were already useful?

I also think evaluation is a big part of the research problem. You need to follow an agent across a sequence of experiences and ask whether it improves, whether that improvement transfers to new situations, and whether it remembers what it learned earlier. That makes continual learning a question about the whole lifecycle of an agent.

I’d want to evaluate agents over long sequences of interactions, where they have to adapt to change while remaining reliable on earlier tasks.

terra-5.6.text:
I think it’s a really central problem if we want agents that can operate in the real world over long periods of time. The setting isn’t, “Here’s a fixed dataset; train once and deploy forever.” An agent is continually encountering new tasks, new environments, and new feedback, and it needs to incorporate that experience without catastrophically forgetting what it already knew.

So there’s this tension between plasticity—the ability to learn something new quickly—and stability—the ability to preserve useful prior knowledge. I’m especially interested in approaches where the agent can build up reusable skills and representations from interaction, and then adapt or compose them when it faces something new. That also raises questions about memory, exploration, and how to tell whether a new experience should change a general belief or just be stored as a specific exception.

It’s hard, but it’s also where the idea of an agent becomes much more compelling: not just a model that answers a prompt, but a system that gets better from its own experience over time.

sol-5.6.text: I think continual learning is one of the central problems for AI agents. An agent operates in a changing world, so it can’t remain frozen after training—it has to learn from new experiences, adapt to new tasks, and build knowledge over time. The difficulty is doing that without catastrophically forgetting what it already knows or allowing a few bad experiences to corrupt its behavior. So the research problem is really about balancing plasticity and stability: deciding what to remember, what to update, and how to consolidate experience into durable knowledge. Memory is a big part of that, but simply storing everything and retrieving it later isn’t enough. We ultimately want agents that can turn experience into improved representations, skills, and decision-making while remaining reliable.

luna-5.6.text: I think continual learning is really about building agents that can improve from experience without erasing what they already know. The challenge is not just adding new facts; it’s deciding what to remember, how to integrate it with existing knowledge, and when to revise beliefs. For agents, that also means learning from feedback over long periods while avoiding drift, shortcut learning, or catastrophic forgetting. I’d like to see research that treats memory, planning, and learning as one system, with clear evaluations of whether an agent becomes more capable and reliable over time—not merely whether it adapts to the next task.

luna-6.text: I think continual learning is one of the central problems if we want AI agents to be useful over long periods. An agent needs to pick up new information from experience and adapt to changing tasks, while still retaining what it learned before. That balance is hard: new learning can interfere with old capabilities, and simply storing more context isn’t the same as learning how to use it. So I’d want to study how agents decide what to remember, how to update their knowledge from feedback, and how to measure whether those updates make them more capable without making them less reliable.
